body:
Why India Developed a Space Programme

India's space programme combines scientific exploration with practical services. Satellites help transmit information across large distances, observe the Earth's surface, monitor weather and provide positioning signals. These capabilities support communication, education, agriculture, natural-resource management and disaster response.

The central idea behind India's early programme was that space technology should contribute to national development. A communication satellite could connect distant villages, while an Earth-observation satellite could help identify crops, water bodies and changes in land use. Scientific research and the development of India's own technological capabilities were pursued alongside these applications.

The Early Institutions and Milestones

Vikram A. Sarabhai is regarded as the founding father of the Indian space programme. He established the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) in Ahmedabad on 11 November 1947. Its early research included cosmic rays and the upper atmosphere. PRL subsequently became an important centre for India's space-science research.

The Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR) was established in 1962 under the Department of Atomic Energy. India's first sounding rocket, a Nike-Apache, was launched from the Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station (TERLS) near Thiruvananthapuram on 21 November 1963. A sounding rocket carries instruments for scientific observations during a short flight; unlike an orbital launch vehicle, it does not place a satellite into a sustained orbit.

The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) was formed on 15 August 1969, replacing INCOSPAR. The Space Commission and Department of Space (DoS) were established in 1972, and ISRO came under the Department of Space.

YearMilestoneSignificance
1947PRL established in AhmedabadFoundation for space-science research
1962INCOSPAR formedOrganised national space research
1963First sounding-rocket launch at ThumbaBeginning of rocket-based experiments
1969ISRO establishedDedicated national space organisation
1972Space Commission and DoS establishedInstitutional framework for space activities
1975Aryabhata launchedIndia's first satellite
1980Rohini RS-1 placed in orbit by SLV-3India demonstrated indigenous orbital launch capability

From Experiments to Applications

Aryabhata, India's first satellite, was launched on 19 April 1975 using a Soviet launch vehicle. It represented an achievement in Indian satellite development, but its launch did not demonstrate an Indian orbital rocket.

That distinction belongs to 18 July 1980, when India's SLV-3 successfully placed the Rohini RS-1 satellite into orbit. The earlier experimental SLV-3 launch in 1979 had not achieved orbit. Therefore, the first Indian satellite and the first successful Indian orbital launch are different milestones.

The Satellite Instructional Television Experiment (SITE) of 1975-1976 demonstrated the use of satellite television for educational and developmental communication. APPLE, launched in 1981, was an experimental communication satellite. IRS-1A, launched in 1988, marked an important beginning in India's operational remote-sensing satellite programme.

What Indigenisation Means

Indigenisation means developing and manufacturing technologies within India instead of depending entirely on foreign suppliers. In the space sector, this includes launch vehicles, satellite structures, propulsion systems, sensors, navigation technology, ground systems and data-processing capabilities.

Indigenisation does not mean that every Indian mission must use only Indian components or avoid international cooperation. Aryabhata was Indian-built but launched abroad; NISAR is a later example of an Indian-American satellite mission. What matters is the capability India develops and the purpose served by cooperation.

Prelims focus

  • Vikram A. Sarabhai is regarded as the founding father of India's space programme.
  • PRL was established in Ahmedabad in 1947.
  • INCOSPAR: 1962; ISRO: 15 August 1969; Department of Space: 1972.
  • Aryabhata: first Indian satellite, launched in 1975 by a Soviet rocket.
  • Rohini RS-1: successfully placed in orbit by India's SLV-3 in 1980.
  • Trap: The first Indian satellite was not the first satellite launched by an Indian rocket.

[NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, chapter 1, The Earth in the Solar System, pp. 1-5, 2018-19 reprint; ISRO, FAQ - About ISRO, questions 1-4; ISRO, Timeline, entries for 1962-1988; Physical Research Laboratory, History, 1947; consulted 4 November 2026.]

title: Origins and Development of the Indian Space Programme

body:
Policy, Research, Manufacturing and Services

India's space activities involve several institutions with different responsibilities. Some formulate policy, some develop rockets and satellites, some distribute data, and others use geospatial information for public services. The distinction between these roles is especially important because several major institutions are located in Gujarat.

The Space Commission provides policy direction for the national space programme. The Department of Space (DoS) implements space programmes mainly through ISRO and associated institutions. ISRO, headquartered in Bengaluru, undertakes the development and operation of space systems and related applications.

Major ISRO Centres

InstitutionLocationMain responsibility
Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC)ThiruvananthapuramLaunch-vehicle design and development
U R Rao Satellite Centre (URSC)BengaluruSatellite design, development and integration
Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR)Sriharikota, Andhra PradeshLaunch-site facilities and rocket launches
Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC)Thiruvananthapuram and BengaluruLiquid and cryogenic propulsion systems
Space Applications Centre (SAC)AhmedabadSatellite payloads, sensors and space applications
National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC)HyderabadEarth-observation data reception, processing and dissemination
ISRO Telemetry, Tracking and Command Network (ISTRAC)BengaluruSpacecraft tracking, telemetry and commands

The Indian Institute of Remote Sensing (IIRS) at Dehradun provides education and training in remote sensing and geoinformatics. The Human Space Flight Centre (HSFC) at Bengaluru is associated with India's human-spaceflight programme. The ISRO Propulsion Complex (IPRC) at Mahendragiri supports propulsion-related testing and activities.

VSSC develops launch vehicles; URSC develops satellites; SDSC-SHAR launches them; SAC develops sensors and applications; NRSC processes and distributes remote-sensing data. These are related stages, not interchangeable functions.

Gujarat's Important Space and Geospatial Institutions

Space Applications Centre, Ahmedabad

SAC is an ISRO centre. Its work includes payloads for communication, navigation and Earth observation, together with methods for using satellite information. It has an important role in developing agricultural and natural-resource applications of remote sensing.

Physical Research Laboratory, Ahmedabad

PRL is a research institution under the Department of Space. Its work includes astronomy, astrophysics, planetary science, atmospheric science and related fundamental research. It is not the national satellite launch site or the principal centre for distributing remote-sensing maps.

IN-SPACe, Ahmedabad

The Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) was established in 2020. Its headquarters was inaugurated at Bopal, Ahmedabad, on 10 June 2022. It promotes and authorises the participation of non-government entities in Indian space activities, subject to the applicable framework. It provides a route for private organisations to undertake authorised space activities; it does not replace ISRO as the national space research organisation.

NewSpace India Limited

NewSpace India Limited (NSIL) was incorporated in March 2019 as a government-owned company under the Department of Space. It is the commercial arm of the Indian space programme, supporting commercial use of space products and services, launch services and greater industry participation. IN-SPACe deals with promotion and authorisation; NSIL deals with commercial activities.

BISAG-N, Gandhinagar

Bhaskaracharya National Institute for Space Applications and Geo-informatics (BISAG-N) is located in Gandhinagar. The earlier Gujarat institution, BISAG, was elevated to national status following the Union Cabinet's 2020 decision. BISAG-N functions as an autonomous scientific society under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY).

BISAG-N develops geographic information systems, thematic maps, geospatial databases and decision-support applications. Its areas include agriculture, water resources, land management, urban planning, education, public infrastructure and disaster management. It combines satellite observations with maps and government records.

BISAG-N's use of space technology does not make it an ISRO centre. Its administrative ministry is MeitY, whereas SAC and NRSC are part of the ISRO system under the Department of Space.

How These Institutions Work Together

Consider a district that needs to identify water-stressed villages. Earth-observation satellites supply imagery. NRSC makes relevant datasets available. SAC may contribute methods for interpreting the observations. BISAG-N or another geospatial agency can combine the imagery with village boundaries, water structures, roads and departmental records. The responsible government department then decides which measures are appropriate.

The satellite provides observations, a geospatial agency develops usable information, and the government department remains responsible for the public decision. This division of work applies to agriculture, urban development and disaster management.

Prelims focus

  • ISRO headquarters: Bengaluru.
  • SDSC-SHAR: Sriharikota; VSSC: Thiruvananthapuram; URSC: Bengaluru.
  • SAC: Ahmedabad; NRSC: Hyderabad; IIRS: Dehradun.
  • PRL: Ahmedabad, under the Department of Space.
  • IN-SPACe headquarters: Bopal, Ahmedabad; NSIL: government-owned commercial company incorporated in 2019.
  • Trap: BISAG-N is under MeitY, not an ISRO centre.

[ISRO, DoS Centres/Units, institutional directory; ISRO, About ISRO, centre functions; Physical Research Laboratory, About and History; IN-SPACe, About and institutional timeline, 2020-2022; NSIL, About Us; Prime Minister's Office, Cabinet approves elevation of BISAG as BISAG-N under MeitY, 2020; BISAG-N, About Us, Profile and Role; consulted 4 November 2026.]

title: Institutions of the Indian Space Ecosystem and Their Roles

body:
Why a Satellite Remains in Orbit

A satellite is an object that revolves around another celestial body. The Moon is a natural satellite of the Earth. An artificial satellite is manufactured and placed into space for communication, observation, navigation or research.

A satellite in Earth orbit is continually attracted towards the Earth by gravity. However, it also has sufficient sideways velocity to keep moving around the Earth rather than falling directly towards the surface. Gravity supplies the force needed to change the direction of its motion.

A launch vehicle, or rocket, carries a satellite towards space and provides the velocity needed to reach the intended trajectory. The satellite and launch vehicle are therefore different objects. A satellite contains a platform, often called a bus, and mission-specific instruments called payloads.

Important Types of Earth Orbit

OrbitMain characteristicTypical purpose
Low Earth orbit (LEO)Relatively close to Earth, generally below about 2,000 kmEarth observation, research and some communication systems
Polar orbitPasses near the polar regions as Earth rotates beneath itObservation of much of Earth's surface
Sun-synchronous orbit (SSO)Observes a location at approximately the same local solar time on successive passesComparable images for mapping and monitoring
Geosynchronous orbit (GSO)Orbital period matches Earth's rotationCommunication and navigation
Geostationary orbit (GEO)Circular, equatorial geosynchronous orbit at about 35,786 km altitude, moving in Earth's direction of rotationContinuous coverage of a fixed region
Geosynchronous transfer orbit (GTO)Elliptical transfer path used before further orbital manoeuvresTransfer towards a higher operational orbit

A geostationary satellite appears nearly fixed above the same point on the equator. It is especially useful for communication and frequent weather observations over a wide region.

Every geostationary orbit is geosynchronous, but not every geosynchronous orbit is geostationary. A satellite in an inclined or elliptical geosynchronous orbit does not remain fixed at one point in the sky. This distinction matters when studying the NavIC constellation.

A sun-synchronous orbit is particularly useful for comparing land-cover and crop images obtained on different days. Observations made at similar local solar times reduce differences caused merely by the changing position of the Sun.

India's Major Launch-Vehicle Families

VehiclePrincipal capabilityImportant distinction
SLV-3Early satellite launch capabilityPlaced Rohini RS-1 into orbit in 1980; retired
PSLVVersatile launches to polar, sun-synchronous and other orbitsWidely used for Earth-observation and scientific missions
GSLVAbout 2-tonne class payloads to GTOUses an indigenous cryogenic upper stage in its developed configuration
LVM3About 4-tonne class to GTO and about 10-tonne class to LEOIndia's heavier-lift launch-vehicle family
SSLVSmall satellites, approximately 500 kg to a 500 km orbitDesigned for relatively quick, demand-driven small-satellite launches

The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) is often called ISRO's workhorse. Its name reflects an important capability, but PSLV is not restricted to polar orbits. It has launched Earth-observation, navigation and planetary missions. The Mars Orbiter Mission and Aditya-L1 were launched by PSLV.

The Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) has a cryogenic upper stage. Cryogenic propulsion uses propellants stored at very low temperatures. Developing an indigenous cryogenic stage was an important step in reducing dependence on imported technology for launching heavier satellites.

LVM3, formerly called GSLV Mk-III, has greater payload capacity than GSLV. It launched Chandrayaan-2 and Chandrayaan-3. A human-rated version of LVM3 is associated with the Gaganyaan human-spaceflight programme.

SSLV is intended for smaller payloads and shorter launch preparation. Its successful SSLV-D3/EOS-08 development flight took place on 16 August 2024. Its development and industrialisation are separate matters from the long-established PSLV and GSLV programmes.

Launch Site and Intended Orbit

India's principal orbital launch site is the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh. It is different from the early sounding-rocket station at Thumba in Kerala.

A successful rocket launch into a transfer orbit does not by itself mean the satellite has reached its final operational orbit. A satellite launched into GTO may subsequently use its own propulsion to reach a geosynchronous or geostationary orbit.

Prelims focus

  • Geostationary altitude: approximately 35,786 km above Earth's equator.
  • Geostationary orbit is a special type of geosynchronous orbit.
  • SSO supports repeated observations at approximately the same local solar time.
  • PSLV is versatile and is not limited to polar satellites.
  • GSLV uses an indigenous cryogenic upper stage; LVM3 has greater payload capacity.
  • Trap: GTO is a transfer orbit, not the final geostationary orbit.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, chapter 10, Gravitation, pp. 131-134, 2018-19 reprint; NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, chapter 1, pp. 4-5; ISRO, Launchers, PSLV, GSLV, LVM3 and SSLV sections; ISRO, Launch Services, orbit and payload-capability descriptions; ISRO, Launch Missions, SSLV-D3/EOS-08 entry; consulted 4 November 2026.]
